How to Use This Book

This book answers every Section B question set in the last three MTE 4103 examinations (term examinations held in 2022, 2023 and 2024, i.e. the 2018, 2019 and 2020 batches). It is arranged by topic, not by year. Each chapter first teaches the theory from the beginning, then solves the past questions on that topic. Each question is quoted exactly as printed on the paper, with its year, number and marks.

The lecture slides of this part are short; the slides themselves say "Never consider lecture slide as study material — follow reference books". The theory here therefore follows the reference books named on the slides: Gonzalez & Woods, Digital Image Processing (main source), Szeliski, Computer Vision, and Davies, Computer and Machine Vision. Everything on the slides is included, and every answer ends with a Source lecture line saying where (or whether) the slides cover it.

■ Theory box
Definitions and results to write in the exam.
■ Formula box
Equations and masks to memorise; all are collected in the Appendix.
■ Exam box

1. Machine Vision Systems ★★★

1.1 What a Machine Vision System Is

Definition (lecture)
A machine vision system (MVS) is the use of a machine to acquire visual information and/or extract information from images for the purpose of data storage or automatic decision making. It deals with the automatic extraction of information from digital images to replace or complement manual inspection and measurement.

Main objective. The objective of a machine vision system is to give an automated machine (a production line, a robot, a sorting gate) the ability to see: to capture an image of a part or scene, extract the required information from it automatically (presence, position, size, identity, defects), and turn that information into a decision or a command — fast, repeatably, without fatigue and without contact. In industry this means:

  1. Quality assurance: 100 % inspection of products at line speed instead of sampling by human inspectors.
  2. Measurement: non-contact dimensional gauging with known accuracy.
  3. Guidance: giving position and orientation (x,y,θ)(x,y,\theta)(x,y,θ) to robots for pick-and-place, assembly and sorting.
  4. Identification and traceability: reading codes, characters and labels.
  5. Data: logging images and measurements for process control and statistics.

A machine vision system is not just software. It is a complete engineering system: lighting, optics, camera, interface, computer, software and an output that acts on the process (Figure 1.1).

1.2 How a Machine Vision System Operates

From the lecture, a machine vision system in operation follows a four-step flow (Figure 1.2):

  1. Imaging — take an image. A sensor detects the part; the camera exposes one frame under controlled lighting.
  2. Processing and analysis — analyse the image to obtain a result. Filter the noise, segment the object, measure or classify it, compare with the tolerance.
  3. Communication — send the result to the system in control of the process (PLC, robot controller, database) through digital I/O, fieldbus or Ethernet.
  4. Action — take action depending on the vision result: reject the part, pick it, stop the line, log the data.

Application types (technical point of view). The lecture divides machine vision applications into four types:

TypeWhat the system doesExamples
LocateFind the object and report its position and orientation.Robot guidance, pick-and-place, bin picking
MeasureMeasure the physical dimensions of the object.Diameter, length, gap, hole spacing in mm
InspectValidate certain features: presence/absence, correctness, defects.Correct label on a bottle, screws in an assembly, chocolates in a box, scratches
IdentifyRead codes and alphanumeric characters for identification.Barcodes, 2-D (DataMatrix) codes, OCR of lot numbers and dates

1.3 Machine Vision, Computer Vision and Image Processing

Three closely related terms are used in this course:

  • Digital image processing (DIP): processing of a digital image by a computer. Mostly image in → image out (enhancement, restoration, compression), extending to segmentation and description.
  • Computer vision (CV): the science of making computers understand images and video — to emulate human vision, including learning, inference and action from visual input. It is a broad, mainly algorithmic and research-oriented field.
  • Machine vision (MV): the engineering application of image processing and computer vision in industry: a complete system of hardware and software that inspects, measures, guides or identifies in a production or automation setting. The lecture: "machine vision systems are fully incorporated with image processing systems, i.e. machine vision is governed by image processing techniques".
The fundamental difference in one sentence
Computer vision is about understanding images in general, usually in uncontrolled environments, and its output is a description or interpretation. Machine vision is about using vision as a sensor inside an automated system, in a controlled environment, and its output is a decision or a control signal (pass/fail, coordinates, a code) produced in real time.
AspectMachine visionComputer vision
GoalAutomate a specific industrial task: inspect, measure, locate, identify; act on the resultInterpret and understand scenes; recognise objects, people, activities
ScopeComplete system: lighting + optics + camera + frame grabber + computer + I/O + actuatorMainly algorithms and software working on given images or video
EnvironmentControlled: fixed lighting, fixed camera distance, known parts, structured backgroundUnconstrained: changing light, clutter, occlusion, viewpoint and scale changes
OutputA decision or command: pass/fail, (x,y,θ)(x,y,\theta)(x,y,θ), a dimension in mm, a decoded stringA description: labels, bounding boxes, segmentation maps, 3-D models, captions
TimingHard real time, tied to line speed (milliseconds per part); deterministicOften soft real time or offline; variable processing time is acceptable
Accuracy / reliabilityVery high repeatability required (e.g. 99.99 % correct, sub-pixel measurements); calibrated in mmStatistical accuracy (e.g. 95 % recognition) is often acceptable; usually uncalibrated
HardwareIndustrial cameras, smart cameras, vision sensors, strobes, PLC interface, rugged enclosuresGeneral computers, GPUs, phones, web cameras, cloud servers
Typical usersManufacturing, packaging, pharmaceuticals, electronics, logisticsAutonomous vehicles, medical imaging, surveillance, AR/VR, internet image search

1.4 Components I: Cameras and Optics

The lecture lists four components of a machine vision system: camera, lighting system, frame grabber, and computer & software. In practice a fifth part — the I/O, communication and actuation link to the process — completes the system (Figure 1.1).

Camera. Machine-vision cameras are digital (not analog as in old video) and fall into three categories:

  1. Vision sensors: a specialised vision system configured to perform one specific task, unlike general camera systems with flexible software. Used for colour sorting, contour verification and text reading. Cheap and simple to set up.
  2. Smart cameras: a camera with a built-in image analysis unit (processor and software inside), so it can operate stand-alone without a PC. Examples from the lecture: the IVC-2D for 2-D analysis (e.g. detecting a misaligned label on a cap) and the IVC-3D, which scans calibrated 3-D data in mm (e.g. a wood surface with defects) and outputs the result.
  3. PC-based systems: the camera captures the image and transfers it to a PC for processing and analysis (e.g. the Ranger C55 high-speed 3-D camera; the "Ruler" 3-D sensor). Most flexible and most powerful; used for complex or multi-camera tasks.

Sensor: CCD or CMOS (Chapter 3), arranged as an area sensor (a full 2-D frame) or a line-scan sensor (one row; the object's motion forms the image — ideal for webs, paper and continuous material). Optics: the lens sets the field of view, working distance, depth of field and distortion. Telecentric lenses give constant magnification with distance (no perspective error) and are used for precise measurement.

1.5 Components II: Lighting, Frame Grabber, Computer and Software

Lighting system. Lighting refers to the light sources and lighting techniques around the object. The object must be clearly visible to the camera: good lighting keeps most of the information in the acquired image, so little image processing is needed and the application becomes simpler and more reliable. In machine vision, lighting is often the most important design decision.

  • Sources: fluorescent tubes, halogen and xenon lamps, LEDs and lasers. LEDs are preferred because of long life, low energy consumption, stable output, choice of colour, and the ability to be strobed (flashed for microseconds) to freeze motion.
  • Lighting types: ring light (around the lens, general illumination), spot light, back light (object between light and camera: a sharp silhouette for edges and dimensions), dark-field light (low-angle light: scratches and engravings shine on a dark background), on-axis (coaxial) light for shiny flat surfaces, dome light (diffuse, shadow-free light for curved or glossy parts), and laser (structured) light — a projected line for 3-D height profiling.

Frame grabber. A device that captures a single frame from an analog video signal (from a video camera or VCR) and stores it as a digital image under computer control. With digital cameras, the modern frame grabber receives the digital stream (Camera Link, CoaXPress, GigE) and buffers it. Its internal blocks are shown in Figure 1.3 and explained in §1.9.

Computer and software. The software typically processes an image in several steps: first it manipulates the image to reduce noise or to convert many shades of gray to a simple combination of black and white (thresholding). After this simplification it counts, measures and/or identifies objects in the image. As a final step it passes or fails the part according to programmed criteria. The lecture lists the elements of a general-purpose image-processing system:

ElementRole
Image sensorsSense the energy radiated by the object and digitise it.
Specialised image-processing hardwareDigitiser plus hardware for primitive operations, e.g. an ALU that does arithmetic on whole images at video rate. Speed is the key parameter (e.g. 30 frames/s).
Specialised image-processing softwareModules that perform specific tasks (filtering, blob analysis, pattern matching, OCR).
ComputerFrom an embedded processor to a supercomputer, depending on the task.
Mass storageEssential: a 1024 × 1024 image with 8 bits per pixel needs 1 megabyte (§3.5).
Image displaysFlat-screen monitors for the operator.
HardcopyLaser printers, film cameras, optical disks for recording images.
NetworkingTransfer of images and results; the key parameter is bandwidth.

I/O and actuation. Trigger sensors (photo-eyes, encoders) tell the system when to take an image; outputs (digital I/O, PLC, fieldbus, Ethernet/IP, TCP/IP to a robot) carry the result to reject gates, diverters and robot controllers.

1.6 Designing a Real-Time Machine Vision System

Design questions (2022 Q5(a), 2024 Q5(b)) expect the components and the engineering constraints. The key relations are:

Machine-vision design relations
Throughput: parts per second =v/p=v/p=v/p (vvv = conveyor speed, ppp = part pitch); the time budget per part is tcycle=p/vt_{\text{cycle}}=p/vtcycle​=p/v; acquisition + processing + output must finish inside it.
Spatial resolution: pixel size on the object Δ=field of viewnumber of pixels\Delta=\dfrac{\text{field of view}}{\text{number of pixels}}Δ=number of pixelsfield of view​ (mm/pixel). The smallest feature or tolerance should span at least 2–4 pixels.
Motion blur: the part moves v tev\,t_evte​ during the exposure tet_ete​. Keep the blur below about half a pixel:  v te≤0.5 Δ ⇒ te≤0.5 Δv\ v\,t_e\le0.5\,\Delta\ \Rightarrow\ t_e\le\dfrac{0.5\,\Delta}{v} vte​≤0.5Δ ⇒ te​≤v0.5Δ​.
Lens: focal length f≈sensor width×working distancefield of viewf\approx\dfrac{\text{sensor width}\times\text{working distance}}{\text{field of view}}f≈field of viewsensor width×working distance​.
Reject timing: if the reject station is a distance ddd downstream, the result must be applied d/vd/vd/v seconds later, i.e. d/pd/pd/p parts later (tracked by an encoder and a PLC shift register).

Other constraints to mention: lighting (uniform, stable, shielded from ambient light; strobed to freeze motion), triggering and synchronisation (part detection, camera and strobe fired together), latency and determinism (worst-case time, not average), robustness (vibration, dust, temperature, enclosure rating), calibration (pixels → mm, camera → robot coordinates), and cost.

Worked feel for the numbers
A belt at v=1.5v=1.5v=1.5 m/s with Δ=0.1\Delta=0.1Δ=0.1 mm/pixel needs te≤0.5(0.1×10−3)/1.5=33 μt_e\le0.5(0.1\times10^{-3})/1.5=33\ \mute​≤0.5(0.1×10−3)/1.5=33 μs. An ordinary 10 ms exposure would smear the image by 1.5×0.01=151.5\times0.01=151.5×0.01=15 mm = 150 pixels. This is why machine vision uses strobed LEDs or very short electronic shutters.

1.7 Past Question: Machine Vision vs Computer Vision

2023 · Q5(a)What is the fundamental difference between machine vision and computer vision? How do the application areas of machine vision and computer vision differ? Explain with necessary examples.15Topic: machine vision vs computer vision

Fundamental difference. Computer vision is the broad scientific field of enabling computers to understand the content of images and video — to recognise, describe and interpret scenes much as humans do, usually in unconstrained, real-world conditions. Machine vision is the industrial engineering application of these techniques: an integrated system of lighting, optics, camera, frame grabber, computer, software and I/O that uses images to make automatic decisions and control a process — inspect, measure, locate or identify parts — in a controlled environment and in real time. In short, computer vision answers "what is in this image?"; machine vision answers "is this part good, where is it, and what should the machine do now?".

The detailed differences are summarised below (write this table in the exam):

AspectMachine visionComputer vision
NatureEngineering system (hardware + software)Scientific/algorithmic field (mainly software)
EnvironmentControlled lighting, fixed geometry, known objectsUncontrolled: varying light, clutter, occlusion, pose
OutputDecision / control signal: pass–fail, (x,y,θ)(x,y,\theta)(x,y,θ), mm, codeInterpretation: labels, boxes, masks, 3-D structure
TimingHard real time, deterministic, synchronised with the lineSoft real time or offline
ReliabilityNear-100 % repeatable, calibrated, traceableStatistical accuracy usually acceptable
IntegrationInterfaces with PLCs, robots, reject actuatorsInterfaces with users, databases, other software

How the application areas differ.

Machine vision applications are found where a machine must act on a part, in factories and logistics. They fall into the four types of §1.2:

  • Inspection: checking that every bottle has a correctly placed label and cap; checking solder joints on PCBs; finding scratches on metal sheets; verifying that all chocolates are in a box.
  • Measurement (gauging): measuring a shaft diameter or a hole spacing in mm on 100 % of parts.
  • Location / robot guidance: giving a robot the position and angle of randomly placed parts for picking (bin picking, depalletising, parcel sorting).
  • Identification: reading barcodes, DataMatrix codes and printed expiry dates (OCR/OCV) on pharmaceutical packs.

Computer vision applications are found where a scene must be understood, often outdoors or in everyday life:

  • Autonomous vehicles: detecting pedestrians, lanes, traffic signs and other vehicles under all weather and lighting.
  • Medical imaging: segmenting tumours in MRI/CT, detecting lesions in X-rays.
  • Security and biometrics: face recognition, people counting, activity recognition in CCTV.
  • Consumer and internet: photo tagging, image search, augmented reality, smartphone camera effects.
Exam tip — the same task, two views
"Recognising a face" in a phone gallery is computer vision; "checking that a printed label on a bottle is straight and rejecting the bottle within 60 ms" is machine vision. One example of each, contrasted like this, earns the "with examples" marks.
Source lectureMT · L1–L2 – Machine vision system (Machine_Vision_MT_L1-L2.pdf, pp. 4–5); L3–L5 – MVS operation & DIP (Machine_Vision_MT_L3-L5.pdf, p. 6) — MV vs CV comparison not in slides; see §1.3

1.8 Past Question: Components; MV vs CV

2024 · Q5(a)What are the major components of a machine vision system? Mention the differences between machine vision and computer vision?10Topic: components of MVS; MV vs CV

Major components (draw Figure 1.1):

  1. Lighting system: LED (preferred), fluorescent, halogen/xenon or laser sources, used as ring, back, dome, dark-field, on-axis or structured light, to make the features of interest clearly visible with high contrast and no shadows or glare.
  2. Camera with lens (image sensor): a CCD or CMOS area or line-scan sensor that converts light into an electrical image; the lens sets the field of view and focus. Cameras are vision sensors, smart cameras or PC-based cameras.
  3. Frame grabber (image digitiser / interface): captures each frame from the camera, converts it to digital form (ADC) if analog, buffers it, and transfers it into computer memory.
  4. Computer and image-processing software: processes the image (noise reduction, thresholding, segmentation, measurement, pattern matching) and makes the pass/fail decision; may include special hardware for speed.
  5. Trigger, I/O and actuation: a part-present sensor triggers the camera and strobe; the result is sent through digital I/O or a network to a PLC, robot or reject mechanism.

Differences between machine vision and computer vision: use the table of §1.7 (environment, output, timing, scope, reliability, applications). Key points: MV is a complete hardware–software system in a controlled environment producing a real-time decision; CV is a broad algorithmic field for understanding images in unconstrained environments.

Source lectureMT · L1–L2 – Machine vision system (Machine_Vision_MT_L1-L2.pdf, pp. 6–17) — MV vs CV comparison not in slides; see §1.3

1.9 Past Question: Components and the Frame Grabber

2023 · Q5(b)What are the components of machine vision system? Discuss about frame grabber as a component of machine vision system.10Topic: components; frame grabber

Components. Camera (vision sensor, smart camera or PC-based camera), lighting system, frame grabber, and computer & software, together with trigger sensors and I/O to the process. Describe each in one or two lines as in §1.8.

The frame grabber. A frame grabber is an electronic board (usually in a PC slot) that captures a single frame from the video signal of a camera and stores it as a digital image under computer control. It is the bridge between the camera and the computer's memory. Its blocks (Figure 1.3) are:

  1. Gain amplifier: amplifies and offsets the incoming analog video signal so that it fills the input range of the ADC (sets contrast and brightness).
  2. Sync separator (synchronisation circuitry): extracts the horizontal and vertical sync pulses from the video, so the grabber knows where each line and each frame starts.
  3. Phase correction (PLL) and acquisition clock: generate a pixel clock locked to the line sync, so every line is sampled at exactly the same positions (no jitter, square pixels).
  4. ADC: samples and quantises the video voltage into digital pixel values (typically 8–12 bits).
  5. Memory buffer (frame store): holds one or more complete frames, so a frame is not lost when the computer bus is busy.
  6. PCI / PCIe bus interface: transfers frames into the host memory by DMA (direct memory access), without loading the CPU.

Why it matters. The frame grabber guarantees loss-free, jitter-free, synchronised image capture at the camera's frame rate (e.g. 30 frames/s or more), supports external triggering (capture exactly when the part is in position), and with digital cameras handles high-bandwidth interfaces (Camera Link, CoaXPress). Some grabbers also do on-board pre-processing (look-up tables, Bayer conversion) to reduce the computer's load.

Source lectureMT · L1–L2 – Machine vision system (Machine_Vision_MT_L1-L2.pdf, pp. 6–17) — frame grabber block diagram on p. 13

1.10 Past Question: Applications and Future Trends

2022 · Q6(d)Mention some applications of machine vision. State some future trends of machine vision.10Topic: applications; trends

Applications of machine vision (group them by the four types of §1.2):

  1. Inspection / quality control: label presence and alignment on bottles, cap and fill-level checks, PCB solder and component inspection, surface defects on steel, glass, textiles and wood, missing screws or parts in assemblies.
  2. Measurement: non-contact gauging of lengths, diameters, gaps and angles; 3-D profiling with laser triangulation.
  3. Robot guidance: pick-and-place, bin picking, parcel and fruit sorting, welding seam tracking, depalletising.
  4. Identification: barcode and DataMatrix reading, OCR/OCV of dates and lot codes, number-plate reading for vehicle access.
  5. Other fields: agriculture (fruit grading, weed detection), food (foreign-object detection), pharmaceuticals (tablet counting), medical imaging, traffic monitoring, security.

Future trends:

  1. Deep learning in machine vision: CNN-based inspection that learns defects from examples instead of hand-written rules; good for natural, variable defects.
  2. Embedded and edge vision: powerful smart cameras with on-board AI processors (GPU/NPU), so the decision is made inside the camera.
  3. 3-D vision: time-of-flight, stereo and structured-light cameras for robot picking and volume measurement.
  4. Hyperspectral, infrared and X-ray imaging for chemical composition, food quality and hidden defects.
  5. Higher speed and resolution: larger CMOS sensors, faster interfaces (CoaXPress, 10/25 GigE), event-based (neuromorphic) sensors.
  6. Industry 4.0 integration: vision data in the cloud for traceability, predictive maintenance and digital twins; easier no-code configuration.
  7. Collaborative and mobile robots guided by vision in warehouses and logistics.
Source lectureMT · L3–L5 – MVS operation & DIP (Machine_Vision_MT_L3-L5.pdf, pp. 6, 14); Sup L3–L5 – Image & digital image (Image and Digital Image - SupL3-L5.pdf, p. 17) — future trends not in slides; see §1.10

1.11 Past Question: Vision-Guided Robot Sorting by Size

2022 · Q5(a)What is the main objective of a machine vision system? Suppose you have got a job at Amazon and you have assigned to build a vision system to sort different size objects by a robot. Now, draw a schematic of a machine vision to sort different size objects by a robot and explain how will it work.18Topic: objective; system design

Main objective. The objective of a machine vision system is to acquire images and automatically extract information from them to make decisions or control a machine — replacing or complementing manual inspection and measurement — with high speed, accuracy and repeatability, and without contact (§1.1). Here the information is the size and position of each object, and the decision is which bin the robot puts it in.

Schematic. Draw Figure 1.4.

Components and their roles:

  1. Conveyor with encoder: carries objects at speed vvv; the encoder reports belt position so every object can be tracked.
  2. Photo-eye (trigger sensor): detects an object entering the inspection zone and triggers the camera and strobe.
  3. Diffuse LED strobe light: shadow-free, uniform illumination; the short flash freezes motion.
  4. Overhead area camera (+ 3-D depth sensor): top view gives length and width; the depth (time-of-flight or laser) sensor gives height. A back-lit belt section is an alternative that gives a clean silhouette.
  5. Frame grabber / GigE interface: transfers each frame to the vision PC.
  6. Vision PC with software: measures and classifies each object.
  7. Robot controller and 6-DOF arm with suction gripper: picks the object at the computed position and drops it into bin S, M or L.

How it works (step by step):

  1. Calibration (once): image a calibration plate to find the scale Δ\DeltaΔ (mm/pixel) and the transformation from image coordinates to robot coordinates.
  2. Trigger and acquisition: the photo-eye detects an object; the camera and strobe fire; the encoder count at that instant is stored.
  3. Pre-processing: median or Gaussian filtering removes noise (Chapter 5).
  4. Segmentation: thresholding separates the object from the belt (Chapter 6); small specks are removed.
  5. Measurement: the object's blob gives its pixel area, a bounding box (length ℓp\ell_pℓp​ and width wpw_pwp​ in pixels), centroid (xc,yc)(x_c,y_c)(xc​,yc​) and orientation θ\thetaθ. Multiply by Δ\DeltaΔ to get mm. Height HHH = (camera-to-belt distance) − (camera-to-top distance) from the depth sensor.
  6. Classification: compute the volume V=ℓ w HV=\ell\,w\,HV=ℓwH (or use the longest side) and compare with thresholds, e.g. small V<1000V<1000V<1000 cm³, medium 1000≤V<10 0001000\le V<10\,0001000≤V<10000 cm³, large V≥10 000V\ge10\,000V≥10000 cm³.
  7. Communication: send the class, the pick point (xc,yc)(x_c,y_c)(xc​,yc​), the angle θ\thetaθ and the encoder count to the robot controller (Ethernet/TCP-IP).
  8. Action: the robot tracks the belt with the encoder, picks the object when it reaches the pick zone, and places it in the correct bin.
Worked example (illustrative numbers)
Camera 1600 pixels across an 800 mm belt  |  object blob 480 × 300 pixels  |  camera-to-belt 1200 mm, camera-to-top 1080 mm

Step 1 — scale. Δ=800/1600=0.5\Delta=800/1600=0.5Δ=800/1600=0.5 mm/pixel.

Step 2 — size. ℓ=480×0.5=240\ell=480\times0.5=240ℓ=480×0.5=240 mm,  w=300×0.5=150\ w=300\times0.5=150 w=300×0.5=150 mm,  H=1200−1080=120\ H=1200-1080=120 H=1200−1080=120 mm.

Step 3 — volume. V=240×150×120=4.32×106V=240\times150\times120=4.32\times10^6V=240×150×120=4.32×106 mm³ =4320=4320=4320 cm³.

Step 4 — decision. 1000≤4320<10 0001000\le4320<10\,0001000≤4320<10000 → medium → bin M

KEY STEPEverything measured in pixels must be converted with the calibration Δ\DeltaΔ before comparing with mm or cm thresholds.

TIMINGIf the belt runs at 0.5 m/s and the robot picks 1.5 m downstream, the object arrives 3 s after the image — plenty of time; the encoder keeps the position exact.
Marks breakdown (18)
Objective (3) · labelled schematic (5) · component roles (4) · step-by-step working with the measure → classify → pick logic (6). A short numeric example like the one above shows real understanding.

1.12 Past Question: Real-Time Bottle-Label Inspection

2024 · Q5(b)You are assigned to design an automated bottle inspection system to detect misaligned labels on bottles moving on a conveyor. Describe, with suitable diagrams, the components and system constraints involved in building such a real-time machine vision system.15Topic: design of a real-time MVS

Components (Figure 1.5):

  1. Conveyor and encoder: move the bottles in single file at constant speed and give their position.
  2. Photo-eye trigger: detects each bottle and fires the camera and light at the same instant, so every bottle is imaged at the same position.
  3. Lighting: a strobed LED ring or diffuse light (a dome light for glossy or curved labels) for high, uniform contrast between label and bottle; a back light can outline the bottle edges.
  4. Camera and lens: an industrial (smart or GigE) CMOS camera with a short electronic shutter; a telecentric or long-focal-length lens reduces perspective error from the curved bottle. For 360° inspection, 3–4 cameras around the bottle, or a bottle rotator.
  5. Vision controller and software: (1) locate the bottle by its edges; (2) segment the label by thresholding or colour; (3) fit straight lines to the label's top and bottom edges (or use pattern matching against a reference label) to get the label angle θ\thetaθ and height yyy; (4) FAIL if ∣θ∣>θmax⁡|\theta|>\theta_{\max}∣θ∣>θmax​ or ∣y−yref∣>Δymax⁡|y-y_{\text{ref}}|>\Delta y_{\max}∣y−yref​∣>Δymax​.
  6. PLC with shift register: holds the pass/fail result until that bottle reaches the reject station (counted by the encoder).
  7. Reject actuator: an air jet or pusher removes failed bottles; a confirmation sensor checks that the reject happened. Results and images are logged.
Assumed design data (to show the constraints quantitatively)
v=1.5v=1.5v=1.5 m/s  |  bottle pitch p=0.1p=0.1p=0.1 m  |  field of view 120 mm on a 1280-pixel sensor  |  tolerance: tilt ±2°, height ±1 mm  |  reject station 0.5 m after the camera

1. Throughput. v/p=1.5/0.1=15v/p=1.5/0.1=15v/p=1.5/0.1=15 bottles/s, so tcycle=1/15=66.7t_{\text{cycle}}=1/15=66.7tcycle​=1/15=66.7 ms. Acquisition + processing + output must take < 66.7 ms in the worst case (design for ≈ 40–50 ms).

2. Resolution. Δ=120/1280=0.094\Delta=120/1280=0.094Δ=120/1280=0.094 mm/pixel. The ±1 mm height tolerance spans ≈ 11 pixels; a 60 mm label edge spans ≈ 640 pixels, so the angle resolution is about tan⁡−1(1/640)≈0.09°\tan^{-1}(1/640)\approx0.09°tan−1(1/640)≈0.09° — well inside ±2°.

3. Motion blur. te≤0.5Δ/v=0.5(0.094×10−3)/1.5≈31 μt_e\le0.5\Delta/v=0.5(0.094\times10^{-3})/1.5\approx31\ \mute​≤0.5Δ/v=0.5(0.094×10−3)/1.5≈31 μs → a strobed LED (or global shutter ≤ 30 µs); a rolling shutter would skew the image of a moving bottle.

4. Reject timing. Delay =0.5/1.5=0.33=0.5/1.5=0.33=0.5/1.5=0.33 s =0.5/0.1=5=0.5/0.1=5=0.5/0.1=5 bottle pitches → the PLC shift register holds 5 results.

ASSUMED DATAThe paper gives no speeds or tolerances; state your assumptions clearly — the examiner marks the method.

CHECKA 10 ms exposure would blur 1.5×0.01=151.5\times0.01=151.5×0.01=15 mm ≈ 160 pixels: the label edge could not be found.

Other system constraints:

  • Real-time determinism: fixed, worst-case processing time; no frame may be skipped; hardware triggering, not software polling.
  • Optical: reflections from glass/plastic and condensation (use diffuse or polarised light); curvature of the bottle distorts the label (telecentric lens, inspect only the central band, or several cameras); depth of field must cover bottle position variation on the belt.
  • Variability: different label designs and bottle colours (recipe-based settings); bottle spacing and orientation variations.
  • Environmental: ambient light (shroud the station, use a band-pass filter matched to the LED colour), vibration (rigid mounting), dust, moisture and temperature (IP65/67 enclosures).
  • Reliability and integration: very low false-reject and zero false-accept rates, reject confirmation, communication with the line PLC, image logging for traceability, and easy changeover.
Source lectureMT · L1–L2 – Machine vision system (Machine_Vision_MT_L1-L2.pdf, pp. 6–14); L3–L5 – MVS operation & DIP (Machine_Vision_MT_L3-L5.pdf, pp. 4–6) — real-time constraints not in slides; see §1.6

2. Digital Images and Digital Image Processing ★★★

2.1 What an Image Is: the Function f(x, y)

An image is a two-dimensional representation of a scene: it records how light reflected or emitted by objects is perceived by a sensor such as the eye or a camera. It represents the variation of brightness (and colour) across a 2-D plane, and is the starting point of every image-processing task. The lecture gives two equivalent definitions:

Definition
An image is a two-dimensional signal, analog or digital, that contains intensity or colour information arranged along the xxx and yyy axes. Mathematically, an image is a two-dimensional function f(x,y)f(x,y)f(x,y), where xxx and yyy are spatial (plane) coordinates, and the amplitude of fff at any pair of coordinates (x,y)(x,y)(x,y) is called the intensity or gray level of the image at that point.

Physically, f(x,y)f(x,y)f(x,y) is proportional to the light energy reaching the sensor from point (x,y)(x,y)(x,y), so it is non-zero and finite: 0<f(x,y)<∞0<f(x,y)<\infty0<f(x,y)<∞. It is the product of the illumination falling on the scene and the reflectance of the scene, f(x,y)=i(x,y) r(x,y)f(x,y)=i(x,y)\,r(x,y)f(x,y)=i(x,y)r(x,y) (derived in §3.1). For a colour image, fff is a vector of three values (fR,fG,fB)(f_R,f_G,f_B)(fR​,fG​,fB​) at each point.

2.2 Analog and Digital Images; Pixels

Analog imageDigital image
Definitionxxx, yyy and the amplitude of fff are continuous quantitiesxxx, yyy and the amplitude of fff are all finite, discrete quantities
ValuesInfinitely many possible values; cannot be stored or processed directly by a computerA finite matrix of numbers; can be stored, transmitted, compressed and processed by a computer
Used forHuman viewingComputer systems
ExamplesPhotographic film, a painting, the image on the retinaA camera's image file, a scanned document

A digital image is a representation of a 2-D image as a finite set of digital values called picture elements or pixels. Pixel values typically represent gray levels, colours, heights, opacities, etc. An analog image is converted to a digital one by sampling (digitising the coordinates) and quantization (digitising the amplitude) — Chapter 3. After digitisation the image is an M×NM\times NM×N matrix:

f(x,y)=[f(0,0)f(0,1)⋯f(0,N−1)f(1,0)f(1,1)⋯f(1,N−1)⋮⋮⋱⋮f(M−1,0)f(M−1,1)⋯f(M−1,N−1)],f(x,y)∈{0,1,…,L−1}.f(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}f(0,0)&f(0,1)&\cdots&f(0,N-1)\\ f(1,0)&f(1,1)&\cdots&f(1,N-1)\\ \vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\ f(M-1,0)&f(M-1,1)&\cdots&f(M-1,N-1)\end{bmatrix},\qquad f(x,y)\in\{0,1,\dots,L-1\}.f(x,y)=​f(0,0)f(1,0)⋮f(M−1,0)​f(0,1)f(1,1)⋮f(M−1,1)​⋯⋯⋱⋯​f(0,N−1)f(1,N−1)⋮f(M−1,N−1)​​,f(x,y)∈{0,1,…,L−1}.

Each element is a pixel. x=0,…,M−1x=0,\dots,M-1x=0,…,M−1 indexes rows and y=0,…,N−1y=0,\dots,N-1y=0,…,N−1 indexes columns, with the origin at the top-left. Resolution is the pixel count M×NM\times NM×N (e.g. VGA 640 × 480 = 307 200 pixels; Full HD 1920 × 1080 ≈ 2.07 million; 4K UHD 3840 × 2160 ≈ 8.3 million). The number of gray levels is L=2kL=2^kL=2k for kkk bits per pixel.

2.3 Types of Digital Images and Formats

TypeBits / pixelValuesTypical use
Binary1 (L=2L=2L=2)0 = black, 1 = whiteMasks, text/document scans, barcodes, shape analysis, segmentation output
Grayscale8 (L=256L=256L=256)0 (black) … 255 (white); one value per pixel, no colourIndustrial inspection and measurement, X-ray, most DIP algorithms
Colour (RGB)24 (8 × 3)Three values R, G, B per pixel; 2563≈16.7256^3\approx16.72563≈16.7 million coloursNatural images, colour sorting and grading, traffic signs
Multispectral / othervariesBands beyond visible light: infrared, satellite bands, depth, medical scansRemote sensing, thermal inspection, 3-D vision

Samples per pixel (lecture): 1 sample (B&W or gray level), 3 samples (red, green, blue), 4 samples (red, green, blue and alpha, i.e. opacity). RGB colour model: each pixel's colour is the additive mixture of R, G and B: R + G = yellow, G + B = cyan, R + B = magenta, R + G + B = white. File formats: JPEG (lossy compression, small files, photographs), PNG (lossless, supports transparency, graphics), BMP (uncompressed raw pixels, large), TIFF (high quality, often lossless; scientific and print use).

2.4 Goals and Applications of DIP

Digital image processing is the processing of digital images by a digital computer. It focuses on two major tasks:

  1. Improvement of pictorial information for human interpretation (enhancement, restoration, colour processing).
  2. Processing of image data for storage, transmission and representation for autonomous machine perception (compression, segmentation, description, recognition).

Applications (lecture): image enhancement/restoration (improve quality, remove noise); remote and space imaging (Hubble telescope images); medical visualisation (MRI scan of a canine heart, finding boundaries between tissues); industrial inspection (product fault detection); law enforcement (fingerprint and number-plate recognition, enhancement of CCTV images); human–computer interfaces (face and gesture recognition); robotics and automation, remote sensing, security and everyday smartphone photography.

2.5 Low-, Mid- and High-Level Processes

There is no sharp boundary where image processing ends and computer vision begins. A useful way to see the whole range is as a continuum of three levels of processing, defined by what goes in and what comes out (Figure 2.2):

LevelInput → outputCharacterExamples
Lowimage → imagePrimitive operations on pixels; both input and output are imagesNoise removal, contrast enhancement, image sharpening
Midimage → attributesPartition the image into regions or objects, describe them in a form suitable for computer processing, and classify individual objects; outputs are attributes extracted from the image (edges, contours, identities of objects)Segmentation, edge detection, object description and recognition of individual objects
Highattributes → understanding"Making sense" of an ensemble of recognised objects; performing the cognitive functions normally associated with visionScene understanding, autonomous navigation

2.6 Past Question: Levels of Process

2022 · Q6(b)The continuum from image processing to computer vision can be broken into- low, medium, and high-level process. Now, explain these levels of process.07Topic: levels of processing

Draw Figure 2.2, then explain:

  1. Low-level process (input: image, output: image). Primitive operations performed directly on pixels, such as noise reduction, contrast enhancement and sharpening. No understanding of the content is involved; the result is a better image. Example: a median filter removes salt-and-pepper noise from a camera image.
  2. Mid-level process (input: image, output: attributes). Tasks such as segmentation (partitioning the image into regions or objects), description of those objects to reduce them to a form suitable for computer processing (area, perimeter, shape), and classification (recognition) of individual objects. The output is a set of attributes — edges, contours, the identity of objects — not an image. Example: thresholding a PCB image and measuring the area of each solder blob.
  3. High-level process (input: attributes, output: understanding). "Making sense" of an ensemble of recognised objects, as in image analysis, and at the far end performing the cognitive functions normally associated with human vision. Example: an autonomous vehicle combining detected lanes, cars and pedestrians to decide to brake.
Source lectureMT · L3–L5 – MVS operation & DIP (Machine_Vision_MT_L3-L5.pdf, p. 13)

LevelBottle-inspection exampleSelf-driving-car example

2.8 Past Question: Fundamental Steps in Digital Image Processing

2022 · Q5(b)What are the fundamental steps in digital image processing? Briefly explain each step with necessary diagram.12Topic: key stages of DIP
  1. Image acquisition: the first step — capturing the image with a sensor and digitising it (sampling and quantization); may include pre-processing such as scaling. e.g. a CCD camera grabbing a frame.
  2. Image enhancement: manipulating an image so that the result is more suitable than the original for a specific application — bringing out obscured detail or highlighting features of interest (contrast stretching, histogram equalization, sharpening). Enhancement is subjective.
  3. Image restoration: also improves the appearance of an image, but is objective: it uses mathematical or probabilistic models of image degradation (blur, noise) to recover the original (e.g. deblurring a motion-blurred photo, Wiener filtering).
  4. Colour image processing: processing using colour models (RGB, HSI, CMY); colour is also used as a basis for extracting features of interest.
  5. Wavelets and multiresolution processing: representing images at several degrees of resolution (image pyramids); the foundation of some compression and analysis methods.
  6. Compression: reducing the storage needed to save an image or the bandwidth needed to transmit it (e.g. JPEG, PNG).
  7. Morphological processing: tools for extracting image components that are useful in representing and describing shape (erosion, dilation, opening, closing, skeletons); e.g. cleaning a segmented fingerprint.
  8. Segmentation: partitioning an image into its constituent parts or objects. One of the most difficult tasks; rugged segmentation brings the process a long way toward a successful solution.
  9. Representation and description: representation decides whether a region is described by its boundary (shape: corners, curvature) or by its interior (texture, skeleton); description (feature selection) extracts the attributes that yield quantitative information of interest (area, perimeter, moments) or that differentiate one class of objects from another.
  10. Object recognition: assigning a label (e.g. "vehicle", "character 7") to an object based on its descriptors.
  11. Knowledge base: prior knowledge about the problem domain (e.g. where defects can occur, what a valid part looks like) is coded into a knowledge base that guides the operation of each module and the interaction between them.

Not every application uses every step; the problem domain decides which are needed. The lecture's version of the diagram omits "wavelets" and shows the remaining blocks in the same arrangement.

Source lectureMT · L3–L5 – MVS operation & DIP (Machine_Vision_MT_L3-L5.pdf, pp. 17–26)

2.9 Past Question: Advantages and Disadvantages of DIP

2022 · Q6(c)Write down the advantages and disadvantages of digital image processing.08Topic: advantages and disadvantages
AdvantagesDisadvantages
  1. Improves the visual quality of an image and the distribution of intensity (contrast, sharpness).
  2. Can easily process a degraded image (noise removal, deblurring, restoration).
  3. Images can be easily modified, copied and processed repeatedly without any loss — results are exactly repeatable.
  4. Image compression reduces the data storage and transmission bandwidth required.
  5. Allows automatic, fast and objective measurement and inspection (machine vision), and processing of images outside the visible band (X-ray, infrared).
  1. Requires a lot of storage and processing power (large, high-resolution images; real-time video).
  2. Environmental conditions (lighting, dust, vibration) may degrade the image quality.
  3. Images contain various types of redundancy — coding redundancy, inter-pixel (spatial) redundancy, psychovisual redundancy — that must be handled.
  4. Segmentation of non-trivial images is one of the most difficult tasks in image processing; results can be unreliable for complex scenes.
  5. Digitisation loses information (sampling and quantization errors), and equipment and expertise can be costly.
Source lectureMT · L3–L5 – MVS operation & DIP (Machine_Vision_MT_L3-L5.pdf, pp. 15–16)

2.10 Past Question: Image as a 2-D Function; RGB, Grayscale and Binary Images

2024 · Q6(a)Define an image formally as a 2D function. Draw distinction among RGB, grayscale, and binary images. Discuss the typical use cases of these images in Digital Image Processing (DIP).08Topic: image as f(x, y); image types

Formal definition. An image is a two-dimensional function f(x,y)f(x,y)f(x,y) where xxx and yyy are spatial coordinates and the amplitude of fff at any (x,y)(x,y)(x,y) is the intensity (gray level) of the image at that point. Physically f(x,y)=i(x,y) r(x,y)f(x,y)=i(x,y)\,r(x,y)f(x,y)=i(x,y)r(x,y) with 0<i<∞0<i<\infty0<i<∞ (illumination) and 0<r<10<r<10<r<1 (reflectance). When xxx, yyy and fff are all finite and discrete, it is a digital image: f:{0,…,M−1}×{0,…,N−1}→{0,…,L−1}f:\{0,\dots,M-1\}\times\{0,\dots,N-1\}\to\{0,\dots,L-1\}f:{0,…,M−1}×{0,…,N−1}→{0,…,L−1} — an M×NM\times NM×N matrix of pixels with L=2kL=2^kL=2k levels.

Typical uses:

  • Binary: output of thresholding/segmentation, object masks and silhouettes for counting and shape measurement, document scanning and OCR, barcodes and QR codes, morphological processing.
  • Grayscale: the default for most machine-vision inspection and measurement (edges and contrast matter, colour does not; 3× less data and faster), medical X-ray, CT and MRI, and the standard input to filters, edge detectors and histogram equalization.
  • RGB: whenever colour carries information — fruit ripeness and food grading, colour sorting, checking printed label colours, skin/face detection, traffic-sign and traffic-light recognition, and display of natural images.

3. Image Sensing, Acquisition and Digitization ★★★

3.1 How an Image Is Formed: Illumination and Reflectance

To generate an image we need an energy source (electromagnetic: visible light, infrared, X-ray, …) and a sensor that detects that energy. The source illuminates the objects; the sensor detects the energy reflected from (or transmitted through) them. Different objects reflect and absorb electromagnetic energy to different degrees, and these differences are why objects appear distinct in the image.

Let i(x,y)i(x,y)i(x,y) be the amount of source illumination incident on the scene point that maps to (x,y)(x,y)(x,y), and r(x,y)r(x,y)r(x,y) the fraction of it that the point reflects. The light reaching the sensor, and hence the image, is the product:

Illumination–reflectance model
f(x,y)=i(x,y) r(x,y),0<i(x,y)<∞,0<r(x,y)<1.f(x,y)=i(x,y)\,r(x,y),\qquad 0<i(x,y)<\infty,\qquad 0<r(x,y)<1.f(x,y)=i(x,y)r(x,y),0<i(x,y)<∞,0<r(x,y)<1. r=0r=0r=0 would be total absorption, r=1r=1r=1 total reflection (black velvet ≈ 0.01, white paint ≈ 0.80, snow ≈ 0.93). For transmitted energy (X-ray), rrr is replaced by a transmissivity. The gray-level range is Lmin⁡=imin⁡rmin⁡≤f≤Lmax⁡=imax⁡rmax⁡L_{\min}=i_{\min}r_{\min}\le f\le L_{\max}=i_{\max}r_{\max}Lmin​=imin​rmin​≤f≤Lmax​=imax​rmax​, shifted to [0,L−1][0,L-1][0,L−1] in practice.

The sensor converts the incoming energy into a voltage by combining the input energy with the electrical response of a material sensitive to that energy (a silicon photodiode for visible light). The output voltage waveform is the sensor response, and a digital quantity is obtained by digitising it.

3.2 Three Sensor Arrangements

(a) Single sensor. A single sensor is a photodiode of silicon whose output voltage waveform is proportional to light. A filter in front of it improves selectivity (e.g. a green filter makes it respond mainly to green light). To produce a 2-D image with a single sensor there must be relative displacement in both the xxx and yyy directions between the sensor and the area being imaged. Example: the film is mounted on a rotating drum (rotation gives one direction) while the sensor moves linearly along the drum's axis (the other direction) — one image line per increment of rotation. Slow, but inexpensive and very high-resolution (precision scanners, microdensitometers).

(b) Sensor strip. Much more common: an in-line arrangement of sensors (a linear strip of e.g. 4096 elements). The strip provides imaging elements in one direction; motion perpendicular to the strip provides imaging in the other direction. Used in flat-bed scanners, airborne imaging, and line-scan cameras over conveyors. Strips mounted in a ring (circular strip) are used in medical and industrial CT: a rotating X-ray source and a ring of detectors give cross-sectional "slices" of a 3-D object.

(c) Sensor array. Individual sensors arranged as a 2-D array (CCD or CMOS) — the arrangement in digital cameras. The response of each sensor is proportional to the integral of the light energy projected onto its surface during the exposure. Because the array is two-dimensional, a complete image is obtained by focusing the energy pattern onto the surface of the array with a lens — no motion is needed. The sensor outputs are then digitised.

3.3 The CCD Image Sensor

Charge-coupled device (CCD) — a silicon integrated circuit on which the image is focused, where the charge at each electrode is proportional to the light exposure. Working principle:

  1. Photon → electron (photoelectric effect): each pixel is a MOS capacitor (potential well). Photons striking the silicon create electron–hole pairs; the electrons collect in the well. The charge is proportional to light intensity × exposure time.
  2. Charge transfer: after exposure, clock voltages applied in sequence to the electrodes move ("couple") each charge packet into the neighbouring well — the whole image shifts down the columns, one row at a time, like a bucket brigade, into a horizontal shift register.
  3. Serial read-out: the horizontal register shifts each packet, one pixel at a time, to a single output amplifier, which converts charge to voltage.
  4. Digitisation: the analog voltage is converted by an ADC outside the sensor (on the camera board), with separate bias, clock and timing circuits.

Properties (lecture): it captures light energy and converts it into digital data recorded by the camera — a "digital version of film"; image quality depends on the sensor resolution; high light sensitivity, clear images; but it consumes more power. Because every pixel passes through the same amplifier, the CCD has excellent uniformity and low noise, but read-out is serial (slower) and fabrication is specialised (costly).

3.4 The CMOS Image Sensor

Complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) sensor, also called an active-pixel sensor (APS). Working principle:

  1. Photon → electron: as in a CCD, a photodiode in each pixel converts captured light into electrons.
  2. Charge → voltage inside every pixel: each pixel has its own transistors (3T or 4T design): a reset transistor (empties the photodiode before exposure), a source-follower amplifier (converts the charge to a voltage at the pixel), and a row-select switch. (4T adds a transfer gate, which enables correlated double sampling to cancel reset noise.)
  3. Addressing: the row decoder selects one row; every pixel in that row places its voltage on its column line. Pixels are therefore read by X–Y addressing, like memory, rather than by shifting charge.
  4. Column amplifiers and ADCs: each column has an amplifier and (in modern sensors) its own ADC, so a whole row is digitised in parallel on the same chip.
  5. Digital output: on-chip timing, control and often image processing; the sensor outputs digital data directly (to a frame grabber or processor).

Shutters. Reading row by row gives a rolling shutter (rows exposed at slightly different times — moving objects look skewed); machine vision prefers global-shutter CMOS sensors, which expose all pixels simultaneously.

FeatureCCDCMOS
Charge-to-voltage conversionOnce, at a single output amplifierIn every pixel
Read-outSerial charge transfer (bucket brigade)Row/column addressing; parallel column ADCs
ADC and logicOff-chipOn-chip ("camera on a chip")
Light sensitivity, noise, uniformityHigh sensitivity, low noise, very uniformTraditionally lower sensitivity, noisier (modern ones are close)
PowerHigh (multi-phase clocks, high voltages)Low
SpeedSlowerFast; windowing (read a region of interest) possible
CostHigher; special fabricationInexpensive — made on any standard silicon production line
Typical useScientific, astronomy, older industrial camerasPhones, most modern industrial cameras, high-speed imaging

3.5 Sampling, Quantization and Resolution

The sensor output is a continuous voltage waveform. To create a digital image, both the coordinates and the amplitude must be digitised (Figure 3.3):

  • Sampling — digitising the coordinate values: dividing the continuous plane into a grid of points. It sets the spatial resolution (M×NM\times NM×N, e.g. 256 × 256, 640 × 480). More samples → finer detail and larger files; too few → blocky, pixelated ("checkerboard") images.
  • Quantization — digitising the amplitude values: mapping the continuous brightness to one of L=2kL=2^kL=2k discrete gray levels. It sets the intensity (gray-level) resolution. More levels → smooth gradients; too few → visible bands (false contouring, "posterisation").
Storage of a digital image
b=M×N×k bits(square image: b=N2k).b=M\times N\times k\ \text{bits}\qquad(\text{square image: }b=N^2k).b=M×N×k bits(square image: b=N2k). Example (lecture): 1024×10241024\times10241024×1024 pixels, 8 bits each: b=10242×8b=1024^2\times8b=10242×8 bits =1 048 576=1\,048\,576=1048576 bytes = 1 MB. A 24-bit colour image of the same size needs 3 MB.

3.6 Image Interpolation

Interpolation is the process of using known data to estimate values at unknown locations. In images it is needed whenever pixels must be created at positions that fall between the existing pixel centres: zooming (resampling to more pixels), shrinking, rotation, geometric correction (removing lens distortion, registration) and resizing for display.

Example: to enlarge a 500 × 500 image to 750 × 750, lay an imaginary 750 × 750 grid over the original; its spacing is 500/750=0.667500/750=0.667500/750=0.667 of the original spacing, so most new grid points lie between old pixels. Their values must be estimated. Three standard methods:

  1. Nearest-neighbour interpolation: assign each new location the value of its nearest pixel in the original image: f(x,y)=f(round(x),round(y))f(x,y)=f(\text{round}(x),\text{round}(y))f(x,y)=f(round(x),round(y)). Simplest and fastest; preserves the original values, but produces blocky, jagged ("staircase") edges when zooming a lot.
  2. Bilinear interpolation: uses the 4 nearest neighbours. The value is v(x,y)=ax+by+cxy+dv(x,y)=ax+by+cxy+dv(x,y)=ax+by+cxy+d, where the four coefficients are found from the four equations at the four neighbours. Equivalently, interpolate linearly along one axis, then along the other (derivation below). Much smoother than nearest neighbour at modest extra cost.
  3. Bicubic interpolation: uses the 16 nearest neighbours (4×44\times44×4): v(x,y)=∑i=03∑j=03aijxiyjv(x,y)=\sum_{i=0}^{3}\sum_{j=0}^{3}a_{ij}x^iy^jv(x,y)=∑i=03​∑j=03​aij​xiyj, with the 16 coefficients from the 16 neighbours. Best at preserving fine detail; the standard in commercial image-editing software.

  1. Along the top row:  f(0,y)=(1−y)f(0,0)+y f(0,1)\ f(0,y)=(1-y)f(0,0)+y\,f(0,1) f(0,y)=(1−y)f(0,0)+yf(0,1).
  2. Along the bottom row:  f(1,y)=(1−y)f(1,0)+y f(1,1)\ f(1,y)=(1-y)f(1,0)+y\,f(1,1) f(1,y)=(1−y)f(1,0)+yf(1,1).
  3. Between the two rows:  f(x,y)=(1−x)f(0,y)+x f(1,y)\ f(x,y)=(1-x)f(0,y)+x\,f(1,y) f(x,y)=(1−x)f(0,y)+xf(1,y).

3.7 Past Question: Digital Image; Formation with a Single Sensor and a Sensor Strip

2022 · Q6(a)Define digital image. Drive the process of a digital image formation from a single sensor element as well as sensor strip.10Topic: digital image; acquisition

Digital image. An image is a 2-D function f(x,y)f(x,y)f(x,y) whose amplitude at (x,y)(x,y)(x,y) is the intensity at that point. When xxx, yyy and the amplitude of fff are all finite, discrete quantities, the image is a digital image: a finite set of digital values called pixels, arranged as an M×NM\times NM×N matrix with L=2kL=2^kL=2k gray levels (§2.2). It is obtained from the continuous scene by sampling and quantization.

Formation with a single sensor element (Figure 3.1(a)):

  1. Light from the illuminated scene (energy f=i rf=i\,rf=ir) falls on a single silicon photodiode, whose output voltage is proportional to the light; a filter in front selects the wavelength band.
  2. A single sensor sees only one point, so a 2-D image needs relative motion in both xxx and yyy. Typically the film/object is on a rotating drum (gives one direction) and the sensor is moved by a lead screw along the drum axis (the other direction).
  3. At each position the sensor voltage is sampled; one rotation gives one image line; the linear step moves to the next line.
  4. Each sample is quantized by an ADC to kkk bits and stored at its (x,y)(x,y)(x,y) address in memory, building the M×NM\times NM×N matrix.

Slow, but cheap and capable of very high resolution because the mechanical motion can be controlled precisely.

Formation with a sensor strip (Figure 3.1(b)):

  1. A linear strip of NNN sensors images a whole line of the scene at once: one direction is "built in".
  2. The object (or the strip) moves perpendicular to the strip, e.g. a document in a flat-bed scanner or parts on a conveyor under a line-scan camera.
  3. At each step of motion the NNN sensor outputs are sampled and quantized, giving one row of NNN pixels.
  4. Successive rows are stacked in memory: after MMM steps the M×NM\times NM×N image is complete. The line rate must match the motion speed so the pixels stay square.
  5. A strip bent into a ring is used in CT: the source rotates and the detector outputs are reconstructed into cross-sectional images.
Source lectureMT · L3–L5 – MVS operation & DIP (Machine_Vision_MT_L3-L5.pdf, pp. 8–9); L6–L7 – Image sensing & acquisition (Machine_Vision_MT_L6-L7.pdf, pp. 6–7)

3.8 Past Question: Image Sensing and Acquisition; CCD and CMOS

2023 · Q5(c)Discuss about the process of image sensing acquisition. Explain the fundamental working principle of CCD and CMOS image sensors.10Topic: acquisition; CCD and CMOS

Image sensing and acquisition. An electromagnetic energy source illuminates the scene; objects reflect and absorb the energy in different amounts (f=i rf=i\,rf=ir, §3.1). The reflected energy is focused by a lens onto a sensor made of a material sensitive to that energy; the sensor converts the incoming energy into a voltage, and the voltage is digitised by sampling and quantization. Three sensor arrangements are used (Figure 3.1): a single sensor with motion in xxx and yyy; a sensor strip with motion perpendicular to it; and a 2-D sensor array (CCD or CMOS) onto which the whole image is focused at once — the arrangement in digital cameras.

CCD working principle (Figure 3.2, left): photons generate electrons that collect in each pixel's potential well, proportional to the exposure; after exposure, clocked electrode voltages shift the charge packets row by row down the columns into a horizontal shift register, which moves them one by one to a single output amplifier (charge → voltage); an external ADC digitises the signal. High sensitivity, low noise and very uniform, but high power and slower serial read-out.

CMOS working principle (Figure 3.2, right): each pixel has a photodiode and its own amplifier transistors; the charge is converted to a voltage inside the pixel; a row is selected and all its pixels drive their column lines; column amplifiers and on-chip ADCs digitise each row in parallel, and the chip outputs digital data. Low power, fast, inexpensive (standard silicon process) and integrated, but traditionally lower light sensitivity and noisier images.

Finish with the comparison table of §3.4 (5–6 rows).

3.9 Past Question: Image Acquisition; the CMOS Sensor in Detail

2024 · Q6(b)What is image acquisition? Explain in detail the working principle of a CMOS-based image sensor.10Topic: acquisition; CMOS

Image acquisition is the first fundamental step of image processing: capturing the light (or other EM energy) from a scene with a sensor and converting it into a digital image. It involves illumination of the scene, formation of the optical image by the lens, conversion of light to an electrical signal by the sensor (single sensor, strip or array), and digitisation by sampling (spatial) and quantization (amplitude) into an M×NM\times NM×N array with LLL levels; it may include simple pre-processing such as scaling.

CMOS sensor — working principle in detail. Draw Figure 3.2 (right) and describe the sequence for one frame:

  1. Reset: the reset transistor of each pixel charges the photodiode to a known reference voltage, emptying old charge.
  2. Integration (exposure): photons absorbed in the photodiode generate electron–hole pairs (photoelectric effect); the collected electrons discharge the photodiode by an amount proportional to light intensity × exposure time.
  3. Charge-to-voltage conversion in the pixel: the in-pixel source-follower amplifier converts the collected charge into a voltage. (In a 4-transistor pixel, a transfer gate moves the charge to a floating diffusion node first; sampling the reset level and the signal level and subtracting them — correlated double sampling — removes reset noise and fixed-pattern offsets.)
  4. Row selection: the row decoder turns on the row-select transistors of one row; each pixel in the row drives its voltage onto its column bus.
  5. Column processing and ADC: a column amplifier and a column-parallel ADC in every column digitise the whole row simultaneously (8–12 bits).
  6. Read-out: the column multiplexer sends the digital values off-chip through a high-speed interface (LVDS, MIPI); the next row is selected, and so on until the frame is complete. On-chip timing and control generate all signals.

Shutter mode: in a rolling shutter the rows are reset and read one after another, so each row's exposure starts at a slightly different time (moving objects appear skewed); a global shutter transfers all pixels' charge to in-pixel storage at the same instant — preferred in machine vision for moving parts.

Characteristics: low power, high speed, region-of-interest read-out, single-chip camera (sensor + ADC + logic), very low cost (any standard CMOS line); historically lower sensitivity and more noise than CCD.

Source lectureMT · L6–L7 – Image sensing & acquisition (Machine_Vision_MT_L6-L7.pdf, pp. 8–9, 11) — CMOS read-out detail beyond the slides; see §3.4

3.10 Past Question: Image Interpolation

2022 · Q5(c)What is meant by image interpolation.05Topic: interpolation

Image interpolation is the process of using known pixel values to estimate intensity values at locations where no pixel exists, i.e. between the original sample positions. It is a basic tool in zooming, shrinking, rotating and geometrically correcting images, where the new pixel grid does not coincide with the old one.

Methods: nearest neighbour (copy the value of the closest pixel — fast, blocky), bilinear (weighted average of the 4 nearest pixels, v=ax+by+cxy+dv=ax+by+cxy+dv=ax+by+cxy+d — smooth), bicubic (16 nearest pixels — sharpest, standard in photo software). Example: with neighbours 10, 20, 30, 40, bilinear interpolation at (0.6,0.25)(0.6,0.25)(0.6,0.25) gives 24.5 (§3.6).

Source lectureNot in the slides — answer built from Gonzalez & Woods (see §3.6)

4. Image Enhancement: Intensity Transformations and Histograms ★★★

4.1 The Objective of Image Enhancement

Definition
Image enhancement is the process of manipulating an image so that the result is more suitable than the original for a specific application. "Specific" is important: a method that is excellent for enhancing X-ray images may not be the best for satellite images. There is no general theory of enhancement — the viewer (or the next machine-vision step) is the judge, so enhancement is subjective and problem-oriented.

Typical goals: bring out detail hidden in dark or bright regions, increase contrast, remove noise, sharpen edges and fine detail, and make features of interest stand out for a human inspector or for the following segmentation and measurement steps.

Enhancement methods work in two domains:

  • Spatial domain — direct manipulation of the pixels:  g(x,y)=T[f(x,y)]\ g(x,y)=T[f(x,y)] g(x,y)=T[f(x,y)], where TTT is an operator defined over a neighbourhood of (x,y)(x,y)(x,y). When the neighbourhood is a single pixel (1×11\times11×1), TTT becomes an intensity (gray-level) transformation s=T(r)s=T(r)s=T(r), also called point processing (rrr = input level, sss = output level). Larger neighbourhoods give spatial filtering (Chapter 5).
  • Frequency domain — modify the Fourier transform of the image (low-pass, high-pass, homomorphic filtering) and transform back.

4.2 Image Restoration and the Degradation Model

Image restoration attempts to recover an image that has been degraded, using a-priori knowledge of the degradation. It is objective: it models the degradation and applies the inverse process, and its success can be measured (e.g. mean-square error against the original).

Degradation / restoration model
g(x,y)=h(x,y)∗f(x,y)+η(x,y)⟺G(u,v)=H(u,v)F(u,v)+N(u,v)g(x,y)=h(x,y)*f(x,y)+\eta(x,y)\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad G(u,v)=H(u,v)F(u,v)+N(u,v)g(x,y)=h(x,y)∗f(x,y)+η(x,y)⟺G(u,v)=H(u,v)F(u,v)+N(u,v) fff = original image, hhh = degradation function (blur from motion, defocus, atmosphere), ∗*∗ = convolution, η\etaη = additive noise, ggg = observed image. Restoration finds an estimate f^\hat ff^​ as close as possible to fff.

Noise models (probability density of the noise values): Gaussian (sensor electronic noise), Rayleigh, Erlang (gamma), exponential, uniform, and impulse (salt-and-pepper) noise (faulty pixels, transmission errors; §5.5). Restoration methods: spatial filters when only noise is present (mean, median, adaptive filters), inverse filtering F^=G/H\hat F=G/HF^=G/H, Wiener (minimum mean-square-error) filtering, constrained least-squares filtering, and blind deconvolution when hhh is unknown.

4.4 The Histogram

The histogram of a digital image with levels in [0,L−1][0,L-1][0,L−1] is the discrete function h(rk)=nkh(r_k)=n_kh(rk​)=nk​, where rkr_krk​ is the kkk-th intensity value and nkn_knk​ the number of pixels with that value. Dividing by the total number of pixels MNMNMN gives the normalised histogram:

pr(rk)=nkMN,k=0,1,…,L−1,∑k=0L−1pr(rk)=1.p_r(r_k)=\frac{n_k}{MN},\qquad k=0,1,\dots,L-1,\qquad \sum_{k=0}^{L-1}p_r(r_k)=1.pr​(rk​)=MNnk​​,k=0,1,…,L−1,k=0∑L−1​pr​(rk​)=1.

pr(rk)p_r(r_k)pr​(rk​) is an estimate of the probability that a pixel has level rkr_krk​. The shape of the histogram reveals image quality: a dark image has its histogram crowded at the low end, a bright image at the high end, a low-contrast image in a narrow band in the middle, and a high-contrast image spreads over the whole range with a fairly uniform distribution. Histogram processing therefore aims to make the histogram cover the full range as uniformly as possible.

4.5 Histogram Equalization, Derived

We look for a transformation s=T(r)s=T(r)s=T(r), 0≤r≤L−10\le r\le L-10≤r≤L−1, that turns any input histogram into a uniform one. Treat rrr and sss as continuous random variables with probability density functions pr(r)p_r(r)pr​(r) and ps(s)p_s(s)ps​(s). TTT must satisfy:

  1. (a) T(r)T(r)T(r) is monotonically increasing in 0≤r≤L−10\le r\le L-10≤r≤L−1 (output levels keep the order of input levels — no reversal of light and dark; strictly increasing makes the inverse unique);
  2. (b) 0≤T(r)≤L−10\le T(r)\le L-10≤T(r)≤L−1 for 0≤r≤L−10\le r\le L-10≤r≤L−1 (output stays in the allowed range).

Step 1 — how a density transforms. The probability that rrr lies in a small interval drdrdr must equal the probability that sss lies in the corresponding interval dsdsds (pixels are only relabelled, not created or destroyed):

ps(s) ∣ds∣=pr(r) ∣dr∣⇒ps(s)=pr(r)∣drds∣.p_s(s)\,|ds|=p_r(r)\,|dr|\quad\Rightarrow\quad p_s(s)=p_r(r)\left|\frac{dr}{ds}\right|.ps​(s)∣ds∣=pr​(r)∣dr∣⇒ps​(s)=pr​(r)​dsdr​​.

Step 2 — choose TTT as the scaled cumulative distribution function (CDF):

s=T(r)=(L−1)∫0rpr(w) dw.s=T(r)=(L-1)\int_0^{r}p_r(w)\,dw.s=T(r)=(L−1)∫0r​pr​(w)dw.

It satisfies (a) because pr≥0p_r\ge0pr​≥0, so the integral never decreases; and (b) because the integral runs from 0 (at r=0r=0r=0) to 1 (at r=L−1r=L-1r=L−1, total probability).

Step 3 — differentiate (Leibniz's rule: the derivative of an integral with respect to its upper limit is the integrand at that limit):

dsdr=dT(r)dr=(L−1)ddr[∫0rpr(w) dw]=(L−1) pr(r).\frac{ds}{dr}=\frac{dT(r)}{dr}=(L-1)\frac{d}{dr}\left[\int_0^{r}p_r(w)\,dw\right]=(L-1)\,p_r(r).drds​=drdT(r)​=(L−1)drd​[∫0r​pr​(w)dw]=(L−1)pr​(r).

Step 4 — substitute into Step 1:

ps(s)=pr(r)∣drds∣=pr(r) 1(L−1) pr(r)=1L−1,0≤s≤L−1.p_s(s)=p_r(r)\left|\frac{dr}{ds}\right|=p_r(r)\,\frac{1}{(L-1)\,p_r(r)}=\frac{1}{L-1},\qquad 0\le s\le L-1.ps​(s)=pr​(r)​dsdr​​=pr​(r)(L−1)pr​(r)1​=L−11​,0≤s≤L−1.

The output density is uniform, whatever pr(r)p_r(r)pr​(r) was. That is why the method is called histogram equalization.

Discrete histogram equalization
sk=T(rk)=(L−1)∑j=0kpr(rj)=L−1MN∑j=0knj,k=0,1,…,L−1,s_k=T(r_k)=(L-1)\sum_{j=0}^{k}p_r(r_j)=\frac{L-1}{MN}\sum_{j=0}^{k}n_j,\qquad k=0,1,\dots,L-1,sk​=T(rk​)=(L−1)j=0∑k​pr​(rj​)=MNL−1​j=0∑k​nj​,k=0,1,…,L−1, then round sks_ksk​ to the nearest integer in [0,L−1][0,L-1][0,L−1]. Every pixel of level rkr_krk​ is mapped to sks_ksk​.

Algorithm: (1) count nkn_knk​ for every level; (2) pr(rk)=nk/MNp_r(r_k)=n_k/MNpr​(rk​)=nk​/MN; (3) cumulative sum ∑j≤kpr(rj)\sum_{j\le k}p_r(r_j)∑j≤k​pr​(rj​) (CDF); (4) multiply by L−1L-1L−1 and round to get sks_ksk​; (5) replace each rkr_krk​ by sks_ksk​; (6) the new histogram: add the nkn_knk​ of all input levels mapped to the same sss.

Properties. Fully automatic — no parameters to choose. Because levels are discrete and rounding merges levels, the result is only approximately flat (some levels become empty, others merge), but the levels are spread over the whole range, which increases contrast. Drawbacks: it can over-enhance noise and wash out images with a large uniform background; histogram matching (specification) and local/adaptive equalization (CLAHE) address these.

4.7 Past Question: Objective of Enhancement; Histogram Equalization

2022 · Q8(a) | 2023 · Q6(a)What is the objective of image enhancement? Describe the method of histogram equalization.10Topic: enhancement; histogram equalization (asked word-for-word in both years)

Objective. The objective of image enhancement is to process an image so that the result is more suitable than the original for a specific application — for human viewing or for further automatic processing. It improves the visual quality or the interpretability of the image: increasing contrast, bringing out detail hidden in dark or bright areas, reducing noise, and sharpening edges. Enhancement is subjective (judged by the viewer) and problem-specific; it does not need a model of how the image was degraded.

Histogram equalization — write §4.5 in this order:

  1. Histogram and normalised histogram pr(rk)=nk/MNp_r(r_k)=n_k/MNpr​(rk​)=nk​/MN; idea: a high-contrast image uses all levels with a roughly uniform histogram, so we want a transformation that makes the histogram uniform.
  2. Conditions on T(r)T(r)T(r): monotonically increasing; 0≤T(r)≤L−10\le T(r)\le L-10≤T(r)≤L−1.
  3. Derivation: ps=pr∣dr/ds∣p_s=p_r|dr/ds|ps​=pr​∣dr/ds∣; choose T(r)=(L−1)∫0rpr(w)dwT(r)=(L-1)\int_0^rp_r(w)dwT(r)=(L−1)∫0r​pr​(w)dw; ds/dr=(L−1)pr(r)ds/dr=(L-1)p_r(r)ds/dr=(L−1)pr​(r); hence ps(s)=1/(L−1)p_s(s)=1/(L-1)ps​(s)=1/(L−1) — uniform.
  4. Discrete form sk=(L−1)∑j=0knj/MNs_k=(L-1)\sum_{j=0}^{k}n_j/MNsk​=(L−1)∑j=0k​nj​/MN, rounded; the six-step algorithm.
  5. Result and remarks: automatic, increases global contrast, histogram only approximately flat; sketch Figure 4.2.
